name: Placement / Building
subtitle: Space rules and feedback loops drive strategy and cascading rewards
demoRuleHint: Example: Select object → Preview highlight → Place → Trigger income/blockage → Adjust layout
problemsSolved: Visualize spatial relationships like tile occupancy and connectivity to reduce cognitive load.
Allow previewing and undoing incorrect placements to reduce frustration and trial‑and‑error waste.
Use layout optimization and cascading rewards to drive ongoing objectives instead of a one‑off placement.
learningGoals: Beginner: understand the layout loop — pick → preview → place → yield/block → adjust — and reproduce an adjacency bonus in the demo
Intermediate: write the occupancy and connectivity contract (grid, snapping, synergy coefficient, expansion cost) and tune the density-vs-yield tradeoff
Advanced: design edge bonuses and risks (defense exposure), and verify spatial-strategy depth with layout-density distribution and expansion-timing distribution
minimalRules: Placement check: object size ≤ 1×1 grid cells and non‑overlapping; size > 1×1 must occupy contiguous cells and not intersect already‑occupied objects.
Connectivity bonus: adjacent same‑type buildings earn +10% income; excessive connectivity accelerates resource consumption, so balance layout density.
Edge bonus: placements on the perimeter earn +5% income; however, they are more vulnerable to attack, so consider defensive layout.
Preview/Highlight: before placement, highlight legal/illegal zones; illegal zones are marked red with a reason to help players correct quickly.
systemLoopHint: Input (Place/Rotate/Move) → Validation (Legal/Illegal) → Feedback (Highlight/Failure Reason) → State Change (Layout Update) → New Input

combos.effect: Arrange resource buildings in high‑yield zones to create a cycle; each resource node must host at least one gathering structure to activate income.
Place defensive towers on the perimeter for a defense bonus; simultaneously place support structures in the center to boost overall defense.
Arrange same‑type buildings along a connectivity line to gain a connectivity bonus; but keep at least one open path to avoid being blocked.

advancedWarnings: Lack of preview and failure reasons will break the placement experience, making it hard for players to judge legal placements.
Too many constraints without sufficient feedback will leave newcomers stuck, steepening the learning curve.
Slow reward settlement reduces perceived strategic payoff, leading players to think the layout is ineffective.
advancedAlgoRefs: Path: path feasibility (walkable/unwalkable) and connectivity checks

demoLab.title: Adjacency Bonus Experiment
demoLab.action: Keep using "Place (primary)" on same-type buildings (as adjacent as possible) and watch synergy and income move together
demoLab.observe: Adjacent same-type buildings grant +10% income — spatial relations translated straight into numbers. The synergy curve lets players see with their own eyes that where you place beats what you place

demoLab.title: Expansion Timing Experiment
demoLab.action: One run: click "Expand (secondary)" twice before placing; another run: fill up without expanding. Compare income after 20 steps
demoLab.observe: Expansion is spending now for space later: too early dilutes current income, too late and slots choke you. Capacity decisions are the invest-vs-spend tradeoff of placement play — the optimum usually sits just before slots fill

demoLab.title: Density Boundary Watch
demoLab.action: Without expanding, fill every slot and watch income growth flatten
demoLab.observe: At full grid, income stalls — density payoff has a boundary, and over-connected layouts burn resources faster. The optimal layout sits at the "dense but not full" edge: that is exactly how spatial constraints manufacture strategy

intro.what: Place buildings or towers onto a limited grid — good placement doubles your income. Tower defense, SimCity, and base-building games are built on this.
intro.feel: You hover a building over the grid, hunting for the highest-yield tile to commit; income ticks upward line by line while you already ponder the next placement — the grid is never big enough.
intro.why: The best demonstration of "space as a resource" — if you want position itself to become strategy, placement play is required study.

concept: Placement play translates spatial relations into numeric yield: adjacency, edges, and density all map directly onto output differences — what players place is not buildings but the shape of a payoff function. The hard part is not what to place — it is previewability and feedback cadence: illegal tiles must explain themselves instantly, and income settlement must show the layout paying off. A player thinks "that placement was clever" because spatial decisions are visible and verifiable.
designNotes: Adjacency bonuses make WHERE beat WHAT: a +10% neighbor bonus digitizes spatial relations — the synergy curve is something players can literally see, and it teaches strategy better than any hidden formula.

Expansion timing is the eternal invest-vs-spend tradeoff: expanding too early dilutes current income, too late and capacity chokes you — the optimum usually hides at the "almost full" edge, and that edge is the decision sweet spot of placement play.

Preview and failure reasons are not accessibility features: illegal placements must highlight red instantly with the reason stated, or players read the rules as bugs — placement UX collapses not from complex rules but from opaque ones.
